name: Narvik
title: Narvik Bulk Carrier Thickness Measurement | Ore Hold UTM
description: Thickness measurement in Narvik for capesize and other bulk carriers loading iron ore: cargo hold, hatch cover, topside and ballast tank gauging.
h1: Cargo Hold and Ballast Tank Gauging for Ore Carriers Loading at Narvik
intro: Narvik exists as a port because of iron ore. LKAB's ore from the Kiruna mine in Swedish Lapland comes by rail along the Ofoten Line to the town's ore harbour, where bulk carriers load in the ice-free Ofotfjord all year round. These ships arrive in ballast with empty holds, often wait their turn, and leave deep-laden for steelworks in Europe and beyond. For a superintendent that is a rare chance to have holds gauged while they are clean and empty, by technicians who fly from India to the ship.

highlights.p: Ore carriers reach Narvik in ballast, often after a long passage, with holds swept at the last discharge port. If the ship has to wait for its berth, hold frames, brackets, hopper plating and tank tops can be gauged before a single tonne of ore is loaded.

highlights.h: Grab damage from the previous port
highlights.p: The heavy grabs that discharge ore at receiving steelworks gouge tank tops and distort lower frames. Narvik is where that damage is visible in clean holds, so it can be measured and photographed before the next cargo covers it again.

Loading follows the delivery of ore trains and the shiploader's programme, so a ship's time alongside can be planned. A scope matched to that programme, holds first and hatch covers as loading proceeds, uses the call without delaying departure.

port.h: Narvik's ore harbour on the Ofotfjord
p: Narvik lies on a peninsula in the Ofotfjord, a deep fjord that opens westwards to Vestfjorden and the open sea. Warm Atlantic water keeps the fjord free of ice through the winter, and that is the reason the port was built: around the turn of the twentieth century, Swedish iron ore needed an outlet that did not freeze, and the Ofoten Line was laid across the mountains from Kiruna to the Norwegian coast. The railway still carries the ore, and LKAB, the Swedish state-owned mining company, runs the ore harbour at Narvik as a sea outlet for production from its Kiruna mine. The town has grown up around the railway, the stockyards and the loading piers. Narvik also has a long wartime history, but it is the ore trains that still set the rhythm of the port.

The ships are bulk carriers, with capesize and other large vessels taking much of the export. Ore pellets and fines are loaded by shiploaders fed from the storage areas beside the piers, and because iron ore is so dense, a loaded ore carrier sails deep with its cargo concentrated in a limited volume, often in alternate holds. Dense ore leaves much of each hold's volume empty, and the loads it places on tank tops, hopper plating and transverse bulkheads are among the highest any cargo produces. Besides the ore harbour, Narvik's public port handles general cargo and transfers between rail and sea at its own terminal, and fishing vessels and cruise ships use the town quays. Most deep-sea traffic is ore, though, and much of the ship-related activity in Narvik is organised around the arrival of the ore trains.

Ships waiting for a loading slot anchor in the fjord or wait off the port until the berth is clear, and waiting time depends on train deliveries, weather and the line-up of ships. Winter brings snow and strong winds funnelling along the fjord, and the town lies well north of the Arctic Circle, so there are weeks around midwinter when the sun does not rise. Neither stops ore loading, but both affect deck work: hatch covers and coamings are cleared of snow and measured under floodlights in winter. In summer the midnight sun allows long, uninterrupted shifts, which suits large hold scopes on ships waiting their turn at the piers. Daylight and weather therefore decide how much open-deck work fits into a call, while hold work runs on regardless.

facilities.h: Where ore carriers are gauged in Narvik
p: The ore harbour is a working loading terminal, not a repair base, so gauging on board is fitted around loading under the terminal's rules and the ship's permit-to-work system. The best window comes before loading begins. A ship that arrives early or waits at anchor can have its holds measured from the tank top with portable lighting, reaching the side frames and brackets that grabs damage most. Once loading starts, work moves to the holds the sequence fills last, to coamings and covers of holds not under the shiploader, and to the deck and engine room. Ballast tanks are full on arrival and emptied as loading proceeds, so any tank entry comes late in the call, after the tanks are drained, ventilated and tested.

Narvik has no dry dock for ships of this size, and ore carriers dock at large yards in Asia, the Middle East or southern Europe, wherever their trading pattern takes them. That makes the Narvik readings particularly useful as a pre-docking steel estimate: an owner who knows hold and tank condition before the ship leaves Norway can order steel and fix the yard specification while the ship is on passage. Ships that return to Narvik on regular contracts can also have a renewal-survey programme gauged in stages over successive calls, so the yard receives a complete picture when the ship arrives.
list: Anchorage and waiting positions in the Ofotfjord — hold frames, brackets, hopper plating and tank tops gauged in clean holds before loading.
Ore loading piers — hatch cover, coaming and deck plating readings on holds not under the shiploader, coordinated with the loading sequence.
Holds the loading plan fills last — tank-top and lower-frame measurements while the first holds are being loaded.
Ballast tanks after deballasting — topside, hopper and double-bottom tank gauging once tanks are empty, ventilated and tested safe for entry.
Public port general cargo terminal — condition and piping gauging on smaller ships lying alongside for longer periods.

context.h: Port state control, bulk carrier rules and the ore trade
p: Ore carriers at Narvik come from many flags and managers, and Paris MoU port state control, carried out by the Norwegian Maritime Authority, often finds them in the middle of a busy loading window. Inspectors look hard at hold structure, hatch covers and side frames, the areas where dense ore cargoes and grab discharge leave their mark. SOLAS chapter XII sets additional structural requirements for bulk carriers carrying dense cargoes such as iron ore, and IACS sets renewal criteria for side frames and brackets in single-side-skin bulk carriers, so the readings taken in a Narvik hold relate directly to rules the ship has to keep meeting.

The economics of the trade point the same way. A capesize carrier arriving in ballast after a long passage has every reason to make use of its time alongside, and an owner who needs a docking steel estimate avoids a separate visit by having the holds measured here. Steelmakers want their ore delivered on schedule, so loading programmes are planned tightly and a gauging team has to fit in without causing delay. Because Norway applies the EU emissions trading system through the EEA, voyages to and from Narvik fall within the scheme, one more reason European charterers watch the age and condition of the ships they fix.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs on ore carriers at Narvik
jobs.p: Narvik jobs almost always involve bulk carriers, and most are built around the time between arrival and the end of loading. Superintendents ask for hold structure first, because that is where damage from the last discharge shows and where surveyors concentrate at the next survey, and add hatch covers, deck and ballast tanks as the call allows. Where an owner is planning a docking after the next voyage, the scope becomes a pre-docking steel estimate, reported quickly enough for the steel order. Results for each hold are passed on as the team finishes it, so the superintendent sees the picture forming during the call. Typical scopes include:
list: A capesize carrier waiting at anchor: side shell frames, brackets and lower hopper plating in all holds, with grab damage measured and photographed.
Hatch cover and coaming gauging, including coaming stays and top plates, on a bulk carrier during loading.
Topside and hopper ballast tank gauging after deballasting, as the final part of a pre-docking steel estimate.
Staged renewal-survey gauging on an ore carrier on a regular Narvik contract, one group of holds per call.
Pre-purchase readings on a large bulk carrier loading its last cargo before handover to a buyer.

logistics: Harstad/Narvik Airport at Evenes is the usual arrival airport, with domestic flights from Oslo and onward road transport to Narvik. The ore harbour is an ISPS facility with its own safety induction, and the ship's agent arranges the team's access with LKAB and the port, as well as launch transport for ships waiting at anchor. Norway is a Schengen state, so technicians travel from India on Schengen visas; because ore carriers' arrival dates firm up only a few days ahead, owners with regular Narvik calls are better served if the visas are kept valid.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while an ore carrier waits at anchor off Narvik?
faqs.a: Yes, if the ship is safe to board by launch and the master agrees. At anchor and in ballast, the holds are empty and the tank top is accessible, which is the best condition for measuring frames, brackets and hopper plating. We bring portable lighting and work through the holds in order of priority in case the ship is called to the berth early.

It should not. Work in any hold stops before the shiploader reaches it, and the team moves to hatch covers, deck, engine room or finished holds as loading proceeds. The plan is agreed with the master and the terminal before the team boards, and the ship's departure always takes priority over completing a non-urgent area.

faqs.q: Are ballast tanks accessible during a Narvik call?
faqs.a: Only late in the call. A ship arriving in ballast has full tanks, which are emptied as cargo goes in. Once a tank is drained, ventilated and tested safe for entry, it can be gauged before departure if time allows; otherwise the ballast tank scope is better done at the discharge port or at the docking yard.

faqs.q: Does polar night or winter weather stop work in Narvik?
faqs.a: Not inside the ship. Holds, tanks and the engine room are measured under artificial light all year. Polar night and snow mainly affect hatch covers and open decks, which need clearing and floodlighting, and strong winds in the fjord can stop launch transfers to the anchorage. We plan winter scopes with time in hand for those delays.
